title: Bhangani in his words
hookLine: he describes the battle of Bhangani in vivid verse (Bachitar Natak 8)
tomorrow: He gave his head, not his faith

lines: THE GURU PICKS UP THE PEN.
cards: War stories usually reach us secondhand. A historian's summary, a movie, an uncle who heard it from someone. Rarely does the person at the center pick up a pen and tell it, beat by beat, in verse.
In Bachitar Natak, Guru Gobind Singh does that for a battle fought at a place called Bhangani. He names the men who stood with him. He writes the noise.
He doesn't hide that arrows came at him too.

teach.h: A HILL KING COMES WITHOUT CAUSE.
teach.b: Here is the outline of his account, in paraphrase. Fateh Shah, a hill king, comes against him, and the Guru writes that he came without cause. The two sides meet.

teach.h: THE VERSE QUICKENS; MEN ARE NAMED.
teach.b: And then the verse changes speed. The meters quicken, the lines clatter like hooves, and the poem names people. His kinsman Sango Shah fights hard and falls.
His uncle Kirpal goes into the fight with a heavy club, and the Guru describes him like a warrior from the old epics.
A chief on the other side, Hari Chand, looses arrows, and the Guru writes that one reached him, and that he answered with arrows of his own.

teach.h: THE COST, THE COMPANIONS, THE GRACE.
teach.b: In the end the hill forces break, and the Guru gives the victory to the grace of the Timeless One. Why is this in a book Sikhs hold sacred? Three things.
First, honesty. He doesn't paint himself as untouchable. He was hit.
Kinsmen died. The cost is in the poem. Second, honor for others.
Kinsmen and companions are named, so they're remembered. Third, the frame from two days ago. This is a scene in the wondrous drama, and its hero isn't him.
He came through, he says, because the One carried him through. Sikh tradition remembers Bhangani as a battle the Guru didn't seek and fought to defend his people.
You don't have to love battle poetry to take something from it. A hard day, told truthfully, names the cost, names who stood with you, and gives thanks for getting to the other side.

how: Sikhs read the account of Bhangani in Bachitar Natak as the tenth Guru's own record of a battle he did not seek, and its names are remembered in katha and Sikh histories.

games.q: what does “bhangani in his words” mean?
o: a ballad sung by soldiers on the losing side
a treaty that ended the fighting in the hills
the Guru's own verse account of a battle he fought

games.q: who's who at Bhangani: tap the pairs.
p: a hill king who came against him
a kinsman who fought and fell
his uncle, with a heavy club
loosed arrows; one struck the Guru

s: in his account, the Guru comes through untouched
he writes that an arrow struck him, and that kinsmen fell.
the verse quickens as the battle begins
the meters change speed, and the lines clatter like hooves.
he gives the victory to his own skill
he gives it to the grace of the Timeless One.

games.q: you're writing your own account of a battle you won. what goes in?
o: the cost, the companions by name, and thanks to the One.
nothing; battles shouldn't be written down.
games.why: the tenth Guru names the fallen and his companions, admits he was struck, and credits the grace of the Timeless One.

practice: Choose one day that was a battle in its own way, a diagnosis, a layoff, a long night in a waiting room, and tell it to yourself the way the Guru tells Bhangani: what it cost, and who stood with you, by name.
Then notice that you're here, on the other side of it. If you pray, rest in Waheguru with thanks on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Bhangani in his words. The tenth Guru's own verse account of a battle: honest about the cost, generous to those beside him, grateful to the One who carried him through. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: through the battle. He came through, and he wrote down who came with him. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Dasam Granth, Bachitar Natak, chapter 8 (the battle of Bhangani: Fateh Shah, Sango Shah, Kirpal, Hari Chand)
